meta.title: "Do it or you'll be sorry" — and your child acts just to make the fear go away | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child to pause in a moment of fear and check: is this a real warning or manipulation? Game-based critical thinking course for children aged 10–16.

hero.headline: Is your child easier to scare than to convince?
hero.subheadline: "Do it or you'll be sorry." "You'll regret it." "Everyone will laugh." Fear hits instantly — and your child acts just to make the feeling go away, without ever checking whether it's even true.

media.alt: A child acting out of fear rather than their own decision

pain.title: Fear isn't an argument — it's a way to switch off thinking
pain.body:
When a child is scared, they don't analyse — they act. The brain switches into "remove the threat" mode, and there's no room left for thinking. This isn't weakness or naivety — it's simply how we react to a strong emotion.

And people use it. Instead of facts, the child is handed a scary scenario: "it'll be bad", "you'll regret it", "you'll end up alone". There's no time to check how real it is. The child just wants the frightening feeling to stop — and does what's wanted of them.

The result — it's not the child making the decision, it's their fear. They agree, refuse, stay silent — not because they decided to, but to get rid of the anxiety faster. And it turns out not to be their choice at all.

solution.title: "Sila Slova" — a detective drama that teaches critical thinking
solution.body: 50 episodes, 13 critical thinking lessons. Your child plays — but is actually learning to protect themselves.
bullets: 🔍 Notices the moment someone tries to push them into acting through fear
🧠 Pauses and asks: "is this a real warning, or am I just being scared?"
💬 Understands: being frightened doesn't mean it's true
🛡️ Decides once the fear has passed — not under its pressure

social_proof.quote: "You'll regret it" used to make my son give in instantly. Now he asks first: "But why exactly would it be bad?" — and sees for himself when he's just being scared.
social_proof.author: Irina, mum of 10-year-old Tim

faq.q: Is it a game or a learning course?
faq.a: Both at the same time. "Sila Slova" looks like a detective series, but every episode contains a hidden critical thinking lesson.

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
faq.a: Ideal for 10–16 year olds. At this age, children are receptive to new thinking patterns and are still forming their views.

faq.q: How much time is needed each day?
faq.a: 15–20 minutes per episode. Flexible schedule — your child can come back at any convenient time.

faq.q: Is registration required for the demo?
faq.a: No. The demo episode is fully open — no registration, no subscription, no personal data required.
